name: ʿAlwa
roles: mother of Muḥammad IV, Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, Fāṭima bint Ismāʿīl, Maryam bint Ismāʿīl
note: Died 1351-06-22 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Bahār
note: Died 1359-03-30 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Yūsuf ibn Muḥammad
note: Died 1362-01-16 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Faraj ibn Muḥammad
note: Died 1365-01-17 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad
note: Died 1363-05-18 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad
note: Died 1351-01-19 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Ibn al-Khaṭīb
note: In the game the ablest man at court (88/79/84). Given command of the host against Aragon in May 1339 (Trent's account). By 8 July 1341 he had left Granada: the save of 8 September 1341 has him in Castile as Frederick ibn al-Khaṭīb, Catholic and Castilian, an admiral from 8 July 1341. On 6 January 1366 he led Castile's last field army, 950 men, at San Clemente, and Murād destroyed it. He himself survived (save of 5 April 1366). Died 1373-03-13 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl
note: Elder brother of Yūsuf I. Regent of Granada from 9 August 1351 until the sultan's return on 7 April 1352, while he made the Hajj (the chronicle's choice; the game named a Naṣr al-Stijjai). Around the new year of 1355 he married Fatiu, daughter of the old ruler of Ghana, fulfilling the Ghana betrothal of 1345, and went south across the desert to live there. His first wife was Shamʿa, of a ruling house of the central Sahara (married 1 March 1354). The chronicle reads his going, like Ismāʿīl's in 1359, as the harem clearing the court of the amir's grown brothers. He died far from Gharnāṭa on 18 September 1370. In August 1395 his son Saʿd was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka (save of 5 August 1395).

name: Yūsuf I
note: Died on 1 August 1363 at Ayamonte, on the march into Portugal in the War of Independence, aged 45, after a reign of thirty years. Father of Saʿd, Ismāʿīl, Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī, Muḥammad, Jadīla, Maryam, Fāṭima, ʿĀʾisha and Umm al-Fatḥ.

name: Fāṭima bint Ismāʿīl
note: Married into the ruling house of the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya (royal marriage of 22 November 1340). Died 1365-06-20 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Maryam bint Ismāʿīl
note: Married into the Karasids of Anatolia (royal marriage of 2 August 1353). Married three times. Back at the court of Gharnāṭa, she took a seat in the dīwān on 10 April 1366, in place of Khālid ibn Yaḥyā, and was set to integrating the new lands (save of 6 November 1366). On 1 October 1370 she turned to promoting Andalusī culture beside Duʿā; by January 1373 she had left the dīwān, and the sultan's mother Sayyida of Fezzan held her seat. Her son by Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad of the Banū al-ʿĀbid, Ismāʿīl, became one of the empire's explorers in 1396. She died on 2 November 1382 (autosave of 1 June 1397).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl
note: Betrothed on 16 March 1354 to a daughter of the Aydınids of Anatolia. He married her about March 1359 and went to live at the Aydınid court, leaving his seat in the dīwān; the chronicle reads it, like Faraj's going, as the harem clearing the court of the amir's grown brothers. He died abroad on 4 October 1380. In August 1395 his son Saʿd, born of his Aydınid wife, was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka (save of 5 August 1395).

name: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Aḥmar
note: Grandson of Muḥammad ibn Faraj of the house of Naṣr, son of Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad (died of the plague, 19 January 1351); called al-Aḥmar, 'the Red', by the game. Husband of the Emperor's half-sister Maryam bint Yūsuf of the dīwān. On 10 February 1396, at sixty-two, he was made an explorer, and by 1 June 1397 he was charting the Canary Islands, sailing from Ishbīliya and lying off Aguere on Tenerife (autosave of 1 June 1397). He died on 24 July 1398, aged sixty-five, a year after he had charted the Canaries (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Sayyida of Fezzan
note: Daughter of the ruler of Fezzan, of the house of Murzuq. Betrothed to Yūsuf on 16 November 1337, aged nine. Her father's name is the game's (name_salmama); its proper form is unconfirmed. Married to Yūsuf I while the Jamāʿa of 1344 sat (Trent's account), a marriage that helped inspire the royal harem law of that October. Mother of Sultan Saʿd, Ismāʿīl and Jadīla. By January 1373 she sat in her son's dīwān, promoting Andalusī culture beside Duʿā (save of 16 January 1373). From 8 March 1378 she worked in the dīwān on the realm's diplomatic endeavours (save of 6 April 1378). She died on 19 November 1380, aged fifty-two (save of 8 December 1382).

name: Gideon ben Joshua
note: A Sephardi Jew of Gharnāṭa, of the burghers' estate; at court by 16 November 1337. Died on 14 May 1339: he fell down the stairs.

name: Yaḥyā Raḥḥū
note: A Zenata Berber, founder and head of the house of Raḥḥū; general from 1 September 1339 at the head of the Volunteers of the Faith. The game calls him 'a competent yet fickle figure'. He led the Volunteers of the Faith again from 18 October 1346, when they rose against the united crowns (in the game files his second command is a separate character with the same name, house and birth date; the chronicle keeps them one man). Took Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl's seat in the dīwān in 1355, after Faraj went to Ghana. Died of illness on 18 February 1355, aged 54 by the game's reckoning, soon after taking the seat; the court called it coincidence.

name: Joan d'Oriola
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Balansiyya
note: Ruler of Valencia from its release as a ṭāʾifa on 23 August 1340: a Catalan, Sunni, of the house the game calls Orihuela. The chronicle keeps the Christian name he was born with, as the game does (Trent's decision), so he stays recognisable later. Died 1368-07-31 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Juan Manuel Enríquez
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya
note: Ruler of Murcia from its release as a ṭāʾifa on 23 August 1340: a Castilian, Sunni. The chronicle keeps the Christian name he was born with, as the game does (Trent's decision), so he stays recognisable later. His host of 410 was destroyed by a Moroccan landing at Málaga on 16 September 1369. Died 1370-06-03 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Khālid ibn Yaḥyā
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Burghush
note: Son of Yaḥyā Raḥḥū and Qamar, the mother of Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl: born into the Raḥḥū house on 30 December 1342. Took his seat in the dīwān on 2 April 1359, at sixteen, after Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl left for the Aydınid court; set to promoting Andalusī culture. One of the ablest men at court (80/85/78), an architect. Left the dīwān on 10 April 1366, when Maryam bint Ismāʿīl took his seat. A general in the Second Marīnid War: he was thrown back before Cádiz on 26 June 1369, held the line at Antequera on 15 October and won at Almuñécar on 8 November (save of 18 November 1369). He went on to win at Adra, Málaga (twice), Jerez and Beja in 1369–1370, the general of the war's second half. By January 1373 married to Charlotte of Crato, a Sunnī Portuguese noblewoman. In January 1402, at fifty-nine and still 80/85/78, he led the crown's Highland Prospecting Survey into the hills, from Almonaster in the Sierra toward El Escorial, Qusanṭīna and home to Ishbīliya (Trent's screens). The survey found iron at al-Iskuriyāl, silver at Qusanṭīna and gems at Qrabaqa, and came home on 3 August 1402. He is one of the court's favourites, sent whenever a member of the house does not see to a thing himself (Trent). On 2 July 1405, at sixty-two, he commanded the joint host of al-Andalus, Aragon and Catalonia, some 20,550 men, that broke the rising of Ciudad Rodrigo at Granadilla (save of 8 July 1405). On 1 November 1411, at sixty-eight, he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Burghush, the 28 towns of Old Castile from Burgos and Valladolid to Palencia, Segovia and Logroño, the first man outside the house of Naṣr to be given a ṭāʾifa (save of 1 November 1411). He died on 2 September 1412, aged sixty-nine, less than a year after he was given Burghush; his son Abū Ḥammū succeeded him (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Alfonso XI of Castile
note: King of Castile, Granada's overlord; husband of Maria, queen of Portugal. He died on campaign on 29 March 1366, a week before the peace that freed Granada (save of 13 September 1370), and his son Jerónimo succeeded him.

name: Maria of Portugal
note: Queen of Portugal in her own right (from 29 January 1342) and consort of Alfonso XI of Castile, the two crowns joined by their marriage. She died of a sudden illness on 4 October 1367, and her son Jerónimo, already king of Castile, inherited Portugal (save of 13 September 1370).

name: Peter of Castile
note: Son of Alfonso XI and Queen Maria, heir to both Castile and Portugal (the 20 May 1343 save). He died of a fever on 11 August 1351, and the double inheritance passed in time to his younger brother Jerónimo.

name: Peter, the Portuguese pretender
note: Queen Maria's younger brother; leads the revolt against her that began on 25 October 1340. Died 1384-06-14 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Najīb
note: A man of the ʿulamāʾ who appears at court by January 1345, with gifts to rival any in the realm (85/96/76). The game calls him Abuna Najīb al-ʿĀbidīn. On 6 October 1351 he was handed over to Castile at its demand, was baptised, and became Ramiro, a Castilian, taking the learning of Qurṭuba's libraries with him: the second great mind of the court to go over to Castile, after Ibn al-Khaṭīb.

name: Saʿd ibn Yūsuf
note: First son of Yūsuf I and Sayyida of Fezzan, born 18 January 1348 in the second year of the war with the three crowns. Betrothed on 19 January 1351 to Aiman, daughter of the Mamluk Sultan. The same winter the Chancellor reported him a Prodigy: a child predestined, the court said, to leave his name in the history books. His father brought the finest tutors of the Islamic world to Gharnāṭa for him, several Christians among them. Succeeded his father on 1 August 1363 at fifteen, under the regency of Naṣr al-Istijjī until he came of age on 18 January 1364. At his accession his abilities stood at 100/69/100, the prodigy fulfilled. His accession was not clean. Naṣr died on the very day the regency ended, of 'sickness' as the court gave out (a hunting accident, the game says), and Saʿd then married Naṣr's widow Duʿāʾ, his father's Marīnid widow and minister. He began his personal rule with two wives, Aiman the Mamlūk and Duʿāʾ the Marīnid. He knocked Portugal out of the War of Independence on 11 September 1364 and took its south, and by 1365 the court called him Conqueror. His first child, Umm al-Fatḥ, was born to Aiman on 13 December 1364. His son and heir Ismāʿīl was born to Duʿāʾ on 8 March 1366. He won the War of Independence on 5 April 1366. He completed the Hajj in 1391 and returned on 20 February 1392 as al-Ḥājj Saʿd. He proclaimed the Restoration of al-Andalus on 16 March 1375 and took the style of Emperor, moved the capital to Ishbīliya in 1379, and fought the three wars of the Istirdād and the crusade of 1404, in which he took Avignon from the Pope. He died on 2 March 1405 (29 Shaʿbān 807), aged fifty-seven, while marching an army through Moya against the risings of 807, after a reign of forty-one years. The game's notice says his strong character had made the country a more honest place (save-day notice of 2 March 1405).

name: Aiman
note: Daughter of the Mamluk Sultan, betrothed to Saʿd ibn Yūsuf, heir of Granada, on 19 January 1351. Married to Saʿd before he came of age; at his majority in January 1364 she was his only wife, until he also married Duʿāʾ. Mother of Saʿd's first child, Umm al-Fatḥ (born 13 December 1364). Mother of Jadīla bint Saʿd (born 13 December 1368). Of the Baḥrī house (the game calls her Aiman Baḥriyya), the house of the Mamlūk sultans: in 1374–1375 its men fought for Granada in Malta and Catalonia, and at court she led the faction of the Mamlūk alliance (Trent's account). As the Emperor's principal wife (consort) the game will not seat her in the dīwān. The chronicle holds that she sits there anyway, by the strength of the harem, without a formal office (Trent's ruling, March 1375). She died on 14 October 1391, aged forty-seven, while the Emperor was on pilgrimage; in the chronicle she died by the Nile on a visit to her family in Egypt (the game's notice says she was attacked by a crocodile), and the court wondered.

name: Duʿāʾ
note: A princess of the Marīnid house of Fās, betrothed to Granada on 18 January 1348 and married to Yūsuf I about 12 August 1354: the one Marīnid bond that outlived Morocco's annulment of its treaties with Granada in 1351. The most capable of the amir's wives, she took Yaḥyā Raḥḥū's seat in the dīwān about 10 March 1355, after his death, under the Powerful Harem law that let women sit in the cabinet. By August 1358 she was widely praised for bringing fresh ideas and practices to the court (the game's 'Foreign Wisdom'), to the nobility's displeasure. Mother of Yūsuf's son Muḥammad (1356–1358). Widowed on 1 August 1363, she married the regent Naṣr al-Istijjī within days. Widowed again a few days after 18 January 1364, when Naṣr died of 'sickness', she then married the young Sultan Saʿd, her late husband Yūsuf's son. That made her his second wife, beside Aiman the Mamlūk. Mother of Saʿd's son and heir Ismāʿīl (born 8 March 1366). While Saʿd campaigned in Aragon in 1374 she ran the court in Gharnāṭa, and with his support by letter summoned the Jamāʿa to give the ʿulamāʾ more power to regulate and tax the dhimmīs (Trent's account). She died on 28 December 1388, aged fifty, after a short illness as the court tells it (the game's death notice gives suicide; the chronicle keeps the court's version, by Trent's ruling).

name: Tizemt
note: A princess of the Ḥafṣid house of Tūnis, betrothed to Granada on 23 July 1345 and married to Yūsuf I on 19 November 1354, three months after his Marīnid marriage. Her name is Berber (Amazigh). Died 1400-03-06 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Fatiu
note: Daughter of the old ruler of Ghana. The Ghana betrothal of 8 September 1345 was fulfilled by her marriage to Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, the amir's elder brother, who went south to live in Ghana with her (around the new year of 1355). Mother of Zineb, Faraj's daughter born in Ghana.

name: Shamʿa
note: Of a ruling house of the central Sahara (the game's AAA43). First wife of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl, by the royal marriage of 1 March 1354, before his second marriage to Fatiu of Ghana. When Faraj went south to Ghana she stayed in Granada with his child. Died 1393-05-10 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: ʿĀʾisha bint Faraj
note: Daughter of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl and Shamʿa, born 28 March 1355 in Granada, about three months after her father had gone south to Ghana. By January 1373 the second wife of her cousin Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf, to whom she bore Muḥammad on 16 November 1372. Died 1408-01-15 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Zineb bint Faraj
note: Daughter of Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl and Fatiu, born in Ghana after her father went south (Fatiu was pregnant in the save of 16 June 1355; the birth date isn't recorded yet).

name: Naṣr al-Istijjī
note: A noble of the house of Istijja (Écija). The game made him regent during Yūsuf I's Hajj (the chronicle gave that regency to Faraj); on Yūsuf's death in August 1363 he became regent for the young Saʿd, and at once married Duʿāʾ, the late amir's Marīnid widow and minister. The game calls him a babbling buffoon. His regency ended when Saʿd came of age on 18 January 1364, and he died that same day. The court called it 'sickness'; the game records a hunting accident. Duʿāʾ, his widow, married the young sultan soon after.

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf
note: Heir to his brother Saʿd until Saʿd's son Ismāʿīl was born on 8 March 1366 (saves of 11 September 1364 and 6 November 1366). Married Hippolyte of Villa di Chiesa, a Sardinian of Cagliari, on 14 September 1370. He took a seat in the dīwān on 1 December 1382, as the revolt of Ṭulayṭula broke out (save of 8 December 1382). He left the dīwān in August 1405, when Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf took his seat, and died on 27 May 1408, aged fifty-four (save of 5 August 1408).

name: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Yūsuf
note: Son of Yūsuf I and Tizemt the Ḥafṣid, born 6 September 1355, the sultan's younger half-brother. At eighteen he led the right wing and two-thirds of the cavalry at the Battle of Barcelona (29 January – 19 February 1374), the wing that broke the Aragonese flank (Trent's account). He died on 29 August 1404 (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Jadīla bint Yūsuf
note: Daughter of Yūsuf I and Sayyida of Fezzan, full sister of Sultan Saʿd. Betrothed on 3 April 1372 to Abū al-Faḍl, son and heir of Abū ʿInān Fāris of Fās (save of 16 January 1373). Married to him by January 1376, when the match helped reopen talks of an alliance between al-Andalus and Fās (Trent's account). Queen of the Marīnids from her husband's accession on 7 October 1381. She died on 27 December 1416, at sixty, three months before her husband; her son Abū Ḥammū had died before her, and her grandson Yaḥyā became sultan of Fās in 1417 (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Maryam bint Yūsuf
note: Daughter of Yūsuf I and Tizemt the Ḥafṣid, younger half-sister of the Emperor Saʿd; a prodigy as a child, and at eighteen the most gifted mind at court by the game's reckoning (99 in administration). Married to Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl al-Aḥmar. Appointed to the dīwān in the reorganisation of the realm after the Restoration of al-Andalus, March 1375 (Trent's account; the save of 16 March 1375 does not show her seat yet). She died on 29 August 1412, aged fifty-five, still in the dīwān, where she had sat since 1396; her seat passed to Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Fāṭima bint Yūsuf
roles: wife of the ḥājib of Catalonia
note: Daughter of Yūsuf I and Tizemt the Ḥafṣid, full sister of Maryam and younger half-sister of the Emperor Saʿd. Married on 15 April 1375 to Francesc de Montsoriu, the ḥājib of the new Ṭāʾifa of Catalonia, binding the house of Naṣr to Barcelona (Trent's account; save of 5 June 1375). Mother of Berenguer Ramon de Montsoriu, ruler of Catalonia, of Isabel, wife of the heir Muḥammad, and of a daughter married to Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl of Shalamanka. She died on 18 September 1409, aged fifty-one (save of 29 June 1410).

name: ʿĀʾisha bint Yūsuf
note: She died on 29 August 1419, at fifty-nine, the last child of Yūsuf I (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Murād
note: Granadan general in the War of Independence. He chased the joined armies of Portugal and Aragon halfway across Iberia and broke them at Zafra on 3 August 1364. Then, on 10 and 11 September, he destroyed their remnants one after the other before Lisbon (save of 11 September 1364). He threw back the Aragonese at Cañete (14 July 1365). At San Clemente (6 January 1366) he destroyed the last Castilian army in the field, commanded by the renegade Ibn al-Khaṭīb (save of 5 April 1366). In the Second Marīnid War he destroyed the sultan of Fās's own force at Cádiz (11 November 1368), threw the first Marīnid landing back into the sea at Marbella (8 February 1369) and retook Jerez (28 April).

name: Umm al-Fatḥ bint Saʿd
note: First child of Sultan Saʿd, born to Aiman the Mamlūk three months after the Portuguese peace. She shares her name, 'mother of victory', with her aunt, Yūsuf I's youngest daughter. By January 1394 she sat in the dīwān, in Duʿā's old seat, integrating the new lands (saves of 1394). She is married to her cousin Saʿd ibn Faraj, who on 5 August 1395 became ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka (save of 5 August 1395). Widowed on 20 February 1408, when Saʿd ibn Faraj died; their daughter Maryam succeeded him in Qūnka. From 24 August 1405 she was integrating the lands won back from the risings (save of 5 August 1408). She died on 25 March 1416, at fifty-one, still in the dīwān (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd
note: Son and heir of Sultan Saʿd, born to Duʿāʾ the Marīnid on 8 March 1366, a month before the Peace of Independence. At eight he was already a silver tongue (63 in diplomacy). In late 1374 he and his half-brother Yūsuf were both given the costly tutors their father had had; his mother Duʿā had wanted them for him alone (Trent's account). On 16 March 1375 he was betrothed to Bernarda of Murcia, the gifted heir of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya, as Murcia was taken into the crown (Trent's account). From 23 August 1385 he ruled as regent while his father made the Hajj, with his mother Duʿā and Aiman quarrelling at court (Trent's account). Before that he had served as an admiral, to carry the crown's authority over the seas: his first command, from 17 June 1383 (save of 1 October 1387) until he joined the dīwān. In 1386 he was brought home, and on 22 January 1387 he took the seat in the dīwān created by the Ḥijāba, to help his father's scholar-building project (Trent's account). He had married Bernarda of Murcia by 1 October 1387. In May 1391 he took a second wife, ʿĀʾisha of the house of ʿOthmān. His sons: Yūsuf (1383–1384) and Muḥammad (born 25 October 1385) by Bernarda; Saʿd (born 17 June 1392) and Aḥmad (born 21 October 1393) by ʿĀʾisha (save of 2 January 1394). By 1398 his sons were Muḥammad, the eldest, judged unfit to rule; Saʿd, intelligent and studious; and Aḥmad, ambitious (Trent's account; save of 3 September 1398). He became Emperor on 2 March 1405, at thirty-eight, when his father died on the march through Moya, and sixteen days later won his first battle as Emperor before Qūnka, destroying the army of the rebel Kingdom of Toledo (Trent's account and screens). On 10 July 1405 he beat the remnant of the Toledo army before Qūnka a second time, and by 24 August 1405 the risings of 807 were over; on 1 September 1405 the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb was taken into the crown. On 1 March 1408 he resolved to raise Qurṭuba as the Capital of the Old Caliphate but kept his court at Ishbīliya (Trent's screen). By August 1408 the game counted him just as well as deceitful and goal-oriented, and he had set aside any thought of changing the succession: his heir Muḥammad's sons would carry the line if he reigned long (Trent's account; save of 5 August 1408). In the fourth war of the Istirdād he led the army himself: at Cuéllar on 13 January 1411 (17 Ramaḍān 813, the day of Badr), 25,700 against Castile's 19,300, and at Toro on 15 May 1411, 20,900 against 11,100; both were victories (Trent's battle screens). He also won at Ledesma (7 March 1411), Besteiros (28 August 1411) and Guimarães (27 October 1411). At the peace of 1 November 1411 he annexed Portugal and took 63 towns from Castile, raising the crown from 161 towns to 258 and its people from 2.04 to 3.96 million (saves of 1 November 1411). Shortly after the Jamāʿa of October 1414 the game also counted him greedy, a ruler who grows iron-fisted and short-sighted in collecting revenue: just in public, deceitful in private, goal-oriented, and now greedy (Trent's screen; the save of 24 October 1414 does not yet show it). His 'silver tongue' is his diplomacy of 100, not a trait.

name: Rodrigo of Silves
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb
note: A Portuguese lord, now a Muslim, set over the Ṭāʾifa of al-Gharb when Granada released the Portuguese south as its vassal on 13 April 1366 (save of 6 November 1366). In September 1368 Castile guaranteed his ṭāʾifa's independence, and Granada backed the loyalists against it. Died 1375-01-24 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Abū ʿInān Fāris
note: Marīnid sultan of Fās. He declared the Second War for the Submission of Granada on 24 October 1368 and led the first Marīnid force across the Strait himself. Murād destroyed it at Cádiz on 11 November 1368 (save of 18 November 1369). He made peace on 12 September 1370 and gave up the whole north shore of the Strait. He died on 7 October 1381 (save of 1 October 1387).

name: ʿUthmān
note: The Marīnid general of the 1369 counterattack. He relieved Cádiz and threw Khālid back before it (2 and 26 June 1369). Then he marched on the heart of the realm and was stopped at Antequera (15 October 1369). Died 1395-01-29 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Jerónimo of Castile
note: King of Castile from his father's death on 29 March 1366, and of Portugal from his mother's on 4 October 1367: the two crowns in a personal union, each keeping its own government. In September 1370 he had no army in the field (save of 13 September 1370). When the union broke in 1389 he kept Portugal. In the War of the League he stood with Castile, and at the Peace of Ramaḍān (22 June 1395) he gave up Lisbon and 19 other towns to al-Andalus (save of 22 June 1395). He died on 29 April 1402, aged fifty-nine, and his son Fernando succeeded him in Portugal (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Fernando of Castile
note: Jerónimo's son and heir, six years old in September 1370. King of Portugal from his father's death on 29 April 1402. In June 1410, at forty-five, he took Portugal into Qashtāla's war against the Emperor Ismāʿīl. His heir is his daughter Joana (save of 29 June 1410). He lost Porto on 7 October 1411 and his kingdom with it: at the peace of 1 November 1411 Portugal was annexed whole by al-Andalus, and Fernando is found at the court of Castile (saves of 1 November 1411).

name: Joan of Aragon
note: King of Aragon and of Sicily (the two crowns in a union since 1343) from 24 April 1368; the game gives him the Catalan form of Juan. His heir in 1370 is his infant daughter Violant. He lost Aragon to the Naṣrids at the peace of 15 March 1375, after the battles of Barcelona and Tarragona and a siege of 282 days, and was let go unharmed to Palermo as a term of the peace, keeping Sicily less Malta. He died on 27 April 1410, aged sixty (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Ibrāhīm II of Tūnis
note: Ḥafṣid sultan of Tūnis, in his current reign from 6 November 1358. In 1370 he ruled the third Regional Power of the Maghrib, with nine subjects, a realm close to disorder (stability near zero), and the Marīnids' fief of Tlemcen as his rival. Died 1399-10-06 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Būlād
note: Sultan of Egypt from the death of his father Jamāl on 3 October 1368, and half-brother of Aiman, Saʿd's Mamlūk wife: Granada's one ally is ruled by the sultan's brother-in-law. In 1370 his realm was the world's seventh power, with some 60,000 men under arms (save of 13 September 1370). Died 1396-06-16 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Muḥammad of the Ottomans
note: Ottoman sultan from 15 September 1364, at sixteen, ruling from Constantinople. In 1370 he was at war with the Anatolian beyliks, with 27,000 men under arms and 73 ships; his brother Murād is his heir. Died 1412-10-01 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Jean II of France
note: King of France from 17 May 1342. By 1370 England's vassals hold much of the old kingdom, his own realm is in disorder (stability below zero), and Castile is his rival. Died 1375-07-19 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Edward IV of England
note: King of England from 18 July 1370. His crown holds more land through its subjects (Wales, Ireland, Aquitaine, Burgundy, Flanders, Brittany and more) than in England itself. Died 1386-07-10 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Charles of Bohemia, Emperor
note: King of Bohemia from 31 May 1340 and Emperor of the 319 members of the Empire. The ablest ruler of Christendom by the game's measure. Died 1379-01-04 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Robert of Anjou
note: King of Hungary, Naples and Croatia, three crowns in one union, from 5 January 1367. Naples leads the Guelph league of Italy; in 1370 his crowns are at war with Halych and Volhynia. Died 1406-06-16 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Pope Abundius
note: Pope from 1 November 1367, sitting at Avignon. Castile's one ally in 1370. Died 1373-11-20 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Hippolyte of Villa di Chiesa
note: Daughter of Xavier, lord of Cagliari in Sardinia, a vassal of Tūnis; Sardinian by culture and Sunnī by faith. Married to the sultan's brother Ismāʿīl on 14 September 1370 (save of 1 November 1370). Died 1405-09-02 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Yūsuf ibn Saʿd
note: Son of Sultan Saʿd and Aiman the Mamlūk, born 15 October 1371, named for his grandfather Yūsuf I (save of 16 January 1373). Following in his father's footsteps, as the court saw it; in late 1374, at three, he was given the same costly tutors as the heir, over Duʿā's objection (Trent's account). Betrothed by October 1387 to Madīna, of a Mamlūk-cultured house, and to Caterina de Borja, daughter of King Alfons of Aragon, he married both, and by January 1394 he had gone to live at the Aragonese court at Benabarre, as the game moves a husband to his wife's court. His children: Muʾmina (born 1389) by Madīna and Saʿd (born 1394) by Caterina, and both wives were with child by him in September 1398. In 1398 he commanded troops for Aragon (March to July). With his mother dead and himself far away, the old quarrel over the succession has cooled (Trent's account; saves of 1 October 1387, 2 January 1394 and 3 September 1398). In September 1398 the Emperor called him home to Ishbīliya with his son Saʿd; Caterina stayed in Aragon (Trent's account). On his brother Ismāʿīl's accession in March 1405 he took Ismāʿīl's old seat in the dīwān, promoting Andalusī culture (save of 31 March 1405). From 7 October 1411 he worked in the dīwān on the realm's standing abroad (save of 1 November 1411). From 27 October 1414, three days after the Jamāʿa, he worked in the dīwān to appease the estates (save of 1 January 1416).

name: Yūsuf ibn Ismāʿīl
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Banbalūna
note: Son of Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf and Hippolyte of Villa di Chiesa, born 19 February 1372 (save of 16 January 1373). A cousin of the Emperor Ismāʿīl. On 1 November 1411 he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Banbalūna, 18 towns of Navarre and the upper Duero, from Pamplona and Tudela to Soria and Medinaceli (save of 1 November 1411). On 1 November 1411 he became ruler of Banbalūna; his son Aḥmad sits in the dīwān. His wives bore him Fāṭima (8 June 1419) and Muḥammad (18 November 1419) (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf
note: Son of Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf and his cousin ʿĀʾisha bint Faraj, born 16 November 1372 (save of 16 January 1373).

name: Charlotte of Crato
note: A Portuguese noblewoman of the house of Crato, Sunnī by faith, married to the general Khālid ibn Yaḥyā by January 1373 (save of 16 January 1373). Died 1395-01-28 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Abū al-Faḍl
note: Son and heir of Abū ʿInān Fāris of Fās. Betrothed to Jadīla bint Yūsuf, the sultan's sister, on 3 April 1372 (save of 16 January 1373). Married Jadīla by January 1376 (Trent's account). Sultan of Fās from 7 October 1381. In June 1410 he answered the Emperor Ismāʿīl's call against Qashtāla with his vassals of Tilimsān and Tafilalt (save of 29 June 1410; Trent's account). He died of pneumonia on 19 March 1417, at fifty-seven, after thirty-five years on the throne. His son and heir Abū Ḥammū, Jadīla's son, had died in a hunting accident on 14 September 1410, during the War of Jillīqiya, so the throne passed to Abū Ḥammū's son Yaḥyā, fifteen, who ruled in his own name from his sixteenth birthday, 14 July 1417 (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Shaykh Ramaḍān of Barqa
note: Ruler of the Sheikhdom of Barqa, a vassal of the Mamlūks, of the Baḥrī house (Baḥriyya) of the Mamlūk sultans; Crimean by culture, Sunnī, 54 years old in 1374, with four wives and eight children. In late October 1374 his army took Malta from Sicily during the War of the Upper March (Trent's account and screenshots). He led Barqa's army in person at Zuwāra (23 May 1374) and Gharyān (24 June 1374), where he destroyed the army of the Jabal Nafūsa, a Sicilian subject (autosave of 1 November 1374). His fleet of eight was sunk by Sicily's off Malta on 12 November 1374. Shortly before the peace of 15 March 1375 he landed 3,000 men in Sicily and stormed Siracusa, which helped persuade King Joan to give up Aragon (Trent's account). Died 1387-01-02 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Dolça d'Oriola
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya
note: Daughter of Joan d'Oriola of Valencia, Sunni. Ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya from 29 January 1371, its ḥājiba in the court's word. Widow of Blai Manrique de Lara, a Muslim scholar who died in November 1372; mother of Bernarda and Estefania. When Murcia was taken into the crown on 16 March 1375 she was granted lands and titles and confirmed as a governor there (Trent's account). Died 1398-01-14 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Bernarda of Murcia
note: Daughter of Dolça d'Oriola and Blai Manrique de Lara, Sunni, heir of the Ṭāʾifa of Mursiyya; a gifted child, Castilian by culture like her father. Murcia's court ties itself closely to the Catalans through its traders. Betrothed to the heir Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd when Murcia was taken into the crown on 16 March 1375. She is being raised at the Castilian court for now, something to watch, though the betrothal holds (Trent's account; save of 16 March 1375, where she sits in Castile). Married to the crown prince Ismāʿīl by 1 October 1387 (save of that date). Mother of Yūsuf (1383–1384) and Muḥammad (born 25 October 1385).

name: Francesc de Montsoriu
roles: ḥājib of the Ṭāʾifa of Qaṭalūniya
note: A Catalan, Sunni, first ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Catalonia, the ḥājib in the court's word, carved from the conquered lands of Aragon around Barcelona on 16 March 1375. On 15 April 1375 he married the Emperor's sister Fāṭima bint Yūsuf (save of 5 June 1375; Trent's account). Died 1394-03-20 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Alfons de Borja
note: A Catalan, Sunni, of the house of Borja; proclaimed king of a renewed Aragon, a ṭāʾifa of the sultan in the interior, on 16 March 1375. The game counts him the fifth Alfons of Aragon, and gives his small kingdom the rank of a kingdom and its seat at Benabarre. The sultan dressed it as a successor to the old crown (Trent's account; save of 16 March 1375). At the peace of 6 April 1378 Castile restored the Aragonese heartland to him, 24 towns with Zaragoza, Huesca, Jaca and Teruel, and his kingdom grew from 6 towns to 30. He died on 24 February 1393. His son Rodrigo (born 1381) succeeded him, with his daughter Caterina as heir (save of 3 September 1398).

name: Alfonso de Oñate
note: The Castilian general of the War of the Aragonese Restoration. He routed the Catalans at Chelva (12 December 1375) and beat the Emperor himself there on 14 January 1376, then lost his army to him at Agramunt on 1 September 1376 (save of 13 January 1377; Trent's battle screens).

name: Khayr al-Dīn al-Jayyānī
note: An Andalusī of Jayyān, Sunni, a courtier at Gharnāṭa, forty in 1391 (birth year estimated from his age). In 1391, under the trade contract with Mali, he was sent to chart the way to Mali along the Atlantic coast instead of across the desert (Trent's account and screenshot).

name: ʿĀʾisha of the house of ʿOthmān
note: An Ottoman princess, Turkish by culture, married in May 1391 to the crown prince Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd as his second wife. Mother of Saʿd (born 17 June 1392) and Aḥmad (born 21 October 1393) (save of 2 January 1394).

name: Pedro of Castile
note: Son of King Fernando, king of Castile from his father's death on 6 January 1394, two months before the Emperor's declaration. He lost the War of the League and on 22 June 1395 surrendered 51 towns, Madrid, Salamanca, Ávila and Cuenca among them, with reparations for ten years (saves of 4 March 1394 and 22 June 1395). In June 1410, at thirty-nine, still king, stubborn and a drunkard, he faced the Emperor Ismāʿīl's declaration of the fourth war of the Istirdād with 1,650 men under arms; his heir is his son Fernando, eighteen (save of 29 June 1410). He capitulated on 2 September 1411, and at the peace of 1 November 1411 gave up 63 towns, Valladolid, Burgos, León and Navarre among them, keeping 45 in the north with his capital at Oviedo (saves of 1 November 1411).

name: Agustín Arce
roles: Grand Master of the Order of Alcántara
note: Castilian, Catholic, fifty in 1394 (birth year estimated from his age), Grand Master of the military Order of Alcántara and general of the Crown of Castile. He led Castile's main army against the Emperor at Ejea de los Caballeros in December 1394 and lost half of it (Trent's battle screens).

name: Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka
note: Cousin of the Emperor Saʿd: son of his late uncle Ismāʿīl ibn Ismāʿīl and of Sevilay, the Aydınid princess Ismāʿīl married in 1359, and raised at least partly at the Aydınid court. On 5 August 1395 he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka, 21 towns of the Leonese west taken from Castile at the Peace of Ramaḍān, with his cousin Saʿd ibn Faraj as his heir. Unmarried and childless in August 1395 (save of 5 August 1395). He died on 15 March 1415, aged fifty-three, and on 11 June 1415 his ṭāʾifa was taken into the crown (save of 1 January 1416).

name: Saʿd ibn Faraj
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka
note: Cousin of the Emperor Saʿd: son of his late uncle Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl and of Shamʿa of the central Sahara. Husband of the Emperor's daughter Umm al-Fatḥ, who sits in the dīwān; their daughters were Maryam (1390–1394) and Jadīla (born 1393). On 5 August 1395 he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka, 20 towns of the Castilian east taken at the Peace of Ramaḍān, with his brother Yūsuf (born 1360) as heir. He is also heir to the Ṭāʾifa of Shalamanka (save of 5 August 1395). He died on 20 February 1408, aged forty-nine, and his daughter Maryam succeeded him as Shaykha of Qūnka (save of 5 August 1408).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad al-ʿĀbid
note: Cousin of the Emperor: son of the Naṣrid princess Maryam bint Ismāʿīl and her second husband Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad (died 1352), lord of a Maghribī house of Tunisian culture, whose head he now is. Born at Gharnāṭa. On 19 February 1396 he was made an explorer, and by 1 June 1397 he was charting southern Macaronesia (the Cape Verde seas), sailing from Coria del Río and last reported off Funchal on Madeira (autosave of 1 June 1397).

name: Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd
note: Eldest surviving son of the crown prince Ismāʿīl, by Bernarda of Mursiyya; born 25 October 1385, while his grandfather was on the road to Makka. By 1398 the game marks him a dull child, and the court thinks him stubborn and unfit to rule (Trent's account; save of 3 September 1398). At seventeen, in July 1403, he stood at 16/20/17, married and with two children; the childhood trait had lapsed with no adult trait in its place (save of 18 July 1403). On his father's accession, 2 March 1405, he became heir to the throne by primogeniture (save of 31 March 1405). Heir to his father from 2 March 1405. By August 1408, at twenty-two, he was married to two daughters of the Catalan ṭāʾifa houses, Magdalena de Borja of Aragon and Isabel de Montsoriu of Catalonia, and had five children: Ismāʿīl (born 4 October 1402) and Saʿd (6 June 1408) by Magdalena, Aḥmad (10 June 1403), ʿĀʾisha (10 March 1405) and a daughter (10 August 1407) by Isabel. Both his eldest sons were gifted, enough to set aside the thought of changing the succession (Trent's account; save of 5 August 1408). On 21 June 1411 he won his first sea battle, at the mouth of the Duero, with 34 ships of al-Andalus and Valencia against Portugal's 17, sinking or taking 15 for the loss of 3. He likes boats (Trent's battle screen and account). By 1416 he had married a third wife, his cousin Jadīla bint Saʿd of Qūnka, who bore him Yūsuf (10 July 1416) and Fāṭima (9 April 1418). By August 1420 the game marks him an extortioner (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd
note: Second son of the crown prince Ismāʿīl, by the Ottoman princess ʿĀʾisha; born 17 June 1392. Intelligent and studious, and given the costly in-depth education of the heirs (Trent's account; save of 3 September 1398). In 1398 the Emperor leaves the succession law as it stands, watching whether this Saʿd grows into a worthy ruler; if not, he means to choose an heir himself (Trent). At eleven, in July 1403, he stood at 56/35/36, still intelligent and on the in-depth education (save of 18 July 1403). At twelve, in March 1405, he stood at 70/37/45, second in line behind his elder brother Muḥammad when their father became Emperor (save of 31 March 1405). By August 1408, at sixteen, he stood at 83/43/61 and was married to his cousin Maryam bint Saʿd, Shaykha of Qūnka, the Emperor's niece; his children, as Trent put it, will rule the frontier. Behind his brother Muḥammad and Muḥammad's sons he is no longer the answer to the succession (Trent's account; save of 5 August 1408). His first son, Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī, was born to Maryam on 17 April 1410 (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Saʿd ibn Yūsuf ibn Saʿd
note: Son of Prince Yūsuf and Caterina de Borja, heir of Aragon; born 18 February 1394 and raised at the Aragonese court at Benabarre with the costly in-depth education. At four he outshines both of the crown prince's sons, and the Emperor wants him raised at his own court (Trent's account; save of 3 September 1398). In September 1398 he was brought to Ishbīliya with his father, to be raised at the Emperor's court (Trent's account). At nine, in July 1403, he stood at 26/24/37, still gifted, now on a military education at the Emperor's court (save of 18 July 1403). He grew up with no adult trait until his twenties; by August 1420 the game marks him deceitful. On 15 December 1417 he took his great-aunt Umm al-Fatḥ's seat in the dīwān, integrating the new lands (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Caterina de Borja
roles: heir of the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon
note: Daughter of King Alfons of the renewed Aragon. Married to Prince Yūsuf ibn Saʿd (betrothed by October 1387, married by January 1394), who went to live at her father's court. Mother of Saʿd ibn Yūsuf (born 1394). Heir to her brother King Rodrigo in 1398, and with child by Yūsuf (save of 3 September 1398).

name: Rodrigo de Borja
roles: king of the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon
note: Son of King Alfons; king of the renewed Aragon from his father's death on 24 February 1393, a boy of eleven. His sister Caterina is his heir (save of 3 September 1398).

name: Maryam bint Saʿd
roles: Shaykha of the Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka
note: Daughter of Saʿd ibn Faraj, ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Qūnka, and of Umm al-Fatḥ, the late Emperor Saʿd's daughter: a niece of the Emperor Ismāʿīl. Married to her cousin Saʿd ibn Ismāʿīl, the Emperor's second son. On her father's death on 20 February 1408 she became Shaykha of Qūnka, at seventeen (save of 5 August 1408; Trent's account). Mother of Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī, born 17 April 1410. By then the game counted her a free thinker (save of 29 June 1410). By August 1420 the game also marks her an entrepreneur (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Ismāʿīl ibn Muḥammad
note: Eldest son of the heir Muḥammad, by Magdalena de Borja; born 4 October 1402, the Emperor's grandson and great-grandson of the Emperor Saʿd. Gifted, and with his half-brother Aḥmad enough at five to set aside the thought of changing the succession (Trent's account; save of 5 August 1408, taken before the boys' educations were set). Grown, by August 1420, into a man of 70/73/63; the childhood gift has lapsed with no adult trait yet in its place (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad
note: Second son of the heir Muḥammad, by Isabel de Montsoriu; born 10 June 1403. Gifted, like his elder half-brother Ismāʿīl (save of 5 August 1408). Grown, by August 1420, into a man of 75/79/70; the childhood gift has lapsed with no adult trait yet in its place (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Magdalena de Borja
note: Daughter of King Alfons of the Ṭāʾifa of Aragon, sister of King Rodrigo and of Caterina, Prince Yūsuf's wife. Wife of the heir Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl and mother of his sons Ismāʿīl (1402) and Saʿd (1408) (save of 5 August 1408).

name: Isabel de Montsoriu
note: Daughter of Francesc de Montsoriu, founder of the house that rules the Ṭāʾifa of Catalonia. Wife of the heir Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl and mother of his son Aḥmad (1403) and two daughters (save of 5 August 1408). Her mother was Fāṭima bint Yūsuf, daughter of Yūsuf I, so Isabel is a granddaughter of the house of Naṣr (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Muḥammad ibn Yūsuf
note: Son of Yūsuf ibn Faraj, the late Faraj ibn Ismāʿīl's son, and of Jadīla, daughter of the Emperor Saʿd: a nephew of the Emperor Ismāʿīl. He took a seat in the dīwān on 24 August 1405, in place of Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf, set to integrating the lands won back from the risings (save of 5 August 1408).

name: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī ibn Saʿd
note: First son of the Emperor's son Saʿd and of Maryam, Shaykha of Qūnka; born 17 April 1410. Through his mother, heir to the frontier ṭāʾifa of Qūnka (save of 29 June 1410).

name: Aḥmad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Burtuqāl
note: Son of Ismāʿīl ibn Yūsuf, the old Emperor's brother: a cousin of the Emperor Ismāʿīl. Married to a daughter of Maryam bint Yūsuf and to a daughter of Khālid ibn Yaḥyā Raḥḥū. On 1 November 1411 he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Burtuqāl, the 34 towns of the old Kingdom of Portugal, with his seat at Barcelos (save of 1 November 1411).

name: Aḥmad ibn Ismāʿīl ibn Saʿd
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn
note: Third son of the Emperor Ismāʿīl, by the Ottoman princess ʿĀʾisha; born 21 October 1393, ambitious as a child. Married to his cousin Muʾmina, Prince Yūsuf's daughter. On 1 November 1411, at eighteen, he was made ruler of the new Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn, 17 towns of the Leonese country from León and Astorga to Zamora and Toro (save of 1 November 1411).

name: Jadīla bint Saʿd
note: Younger daughter of Saʿd ibn Faraj of Qūnka and Umm al-Fatḥ, sister of the Shaykha Maryam. Married to the heir Muḥammad ibn Ismāʿīl, his third wife. On 2 January 1412 she took a seat in the dīwān, set to encouraging migration (save of 24 October 1414). From 29 September 1416 she sat in the dīwān as its steward of the realm's peace, stabilising the country. She bore the heir two children: Yūsuf, on 10 July 1416, and Fāṭima, on 9 April 1418 (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Aḥmad ibn Yūsuf
note: Son of Yūsuf ibn Ismāʿīl, ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Banbalūna; one of the ablest men of the house. He took Maryam bint Yūsuf's seat in the dīwān after her death in August 1412, set to integrating the new lands (save of 24 October 1414). By 1420 he was married to two daughters of his cousin Aḥmad of Burtuqāl, Fāṭima and Maryam, and had three children: Abū al-Ḥasan ʿAlī (16 February 1417), Muʾmina (13 August 1417) and Saʿd (27 July 1419). The game marks him unmotivated (save of 11 August 1420).

name: Abū Ḥammū ibn Khālid Raḥḥū
roles: ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Burghush
note: Son of Khālid ibn Yaḥyā Raḥḥū. He succeeded his father as ruler of the Ṭāʾifa of Burghush on 2 September 1412 (save of 24 October 1414).

name: Tīmūr
note: Lord of Samarqand from 25 October 1360. Between 1394 and 1420 his realm grew from 234 towns to 707, the fourth power of the world: Herat, Iṣfahān and Tabrīz by 1407, Kāshghar and Farghāna in February 1414, Fārs, Kirmān and Hurmuz in 1415. In August 1420 he was eighty-four and still on the throne; his chosen heir was Köke, a conqueror and army reformer of forty-eight (world files of 1394–1420).

name: Aḥmad
note: Son of the Ottoman sultan Muḥammad and brother of ʿĀʾisha, the Emperor Ismāʿīl's wife. Sultan from his father's death of old age on 1 October 1412. A zealot of little ability (17/14/20), but his peace of April 1417 took Sivas and the lands of Eretna, Amasya and the Dobruja; in 1420 his realm held 294 towns and 82 ships, sixth in the world. His heir is his son Murād, born 7 November 1393, a far better diplomat (world file of 11 August 1420).

name: Aqṭāy
note: Son of the sultan Būlād, whom he succeeded on 16 June 1396. Al-Andalus's one ally in the East since 1367. In 1420 he ruled 191 towns from Cairo and 103 more through vassals from the Ḥijāz to the Taurus, ninth in the world; Hungary, the Ottomans and the Tīmūrids are his rivals. His heir is his son Jyral, born 30 December 1401 (world file of 11 August 1420).

name: Yaḥyā
note: Son of Abū Ḥammū and grandson of Abū al-Faḍl of Fās and Jadīla bint Yūsuf, so a great-grandson of Yūsuf I of Gharnāṭa. His father died in a hunting accident in 1410; he succeeded his grandfather on 19 March 1417 and ruled in his own name from his sixteenth birthday, 14 July 1417. Fās stays allied to al-Andalus (world file of 11 August 1420).

name: Eduardo de Avellaneda
note: A Castilian Catholic noble who led the rising of the province of Zamora against the Ṭāʾifa of Liyūn on 1 June 1420. The Emperor Ismāʿīl destroyed his 370 men at Fermoselle on 10 August 1420 without the loss of a man (save of 11 August 1420).
